signature_name[len] is a plain char passed to isspace without an (unsigned char) cast; for bytes > 0x7F in a signed-char build this is technically undefined per the C standard, though benign on glibc/MSVC implementations — no demonstrable out-of-bounds or disclosure.

The cert_name prefix whitelist (lines 17-21) is advisory UX: on user-YES the code still performs full WinVerifyTrust validation, so a whitelist bypass alone grants nothing; an empty cert_name entry would match any signature, but that is a configuration concern, not a defect in this code.

verdict.summary: This r2 comment-command handler is not vulnerable to a direct security impact. The only memory-copy sink (case '+') is guarded by an allocation sized from the same string whose length dominates the copy target, and r_str_unescape is provably length-non-increasing, so the buffer always suffices. All callee sentinel returns that gate use (r_meta_get_string, sdb_decode, r_str_between, r_core_editor) are tested before first use. The remaining anomalies are unchecked strdup/malloc-failure NULL dereferences that merely crash the same-privilege CLI process and are robustness issues, not vulnerabilities.

assumptions: input is a NUL-terminated command string routed here only for commands beginning with 'C', so input[1] is always readable.

r_str_unescape is length-non-increasing (each escape sequence of >=2 source chars maps to <=1 output char), so strlen(nc) <= strlen(newcomment) and the malloc sized by strlen(comment)+strlen(newcomment)+2 dominates the strcpy/strcat concatenation.
r_num_math and the r_meta_* / r_cons_* APIs consume values within their own documented domains; no raw attacker size/index/offset is passed into a memory operation in this code.
limitations: Unchecked allocation sentinel: 'char *nc = strdup (newcomment); r_str_unescape (nc);' and later 'strcat (text, nc)' (case '+'), and 's = strdup (s + 1); p = strchr (s, ' ');' (case 'a') use strdup's return without a NULL test; an allocation failure (e.g., an impractically huge typed comment) causes a same-privilege crash (CWE-476 robustness), not memory corruption.

Case '+'/' ' undo path builds an r2 command string from raw user text via 'r_str_newf ("CC %s@0x%08"PFMT64x, nc, addr)' and pushes it as an undo action; if that text were ever sourced across a trust boundary (e.g., replayed from a project/script file), executing undo could inject r2 commands (CWE-78 shape). In this code the text originates from the same-privilege CLI user's own typed command and the undo-execution path is not shown, so the impact is not instantiated here.
Both switch statements lack a default arm; unrecognized 'CC' subcommands silently fall through with no action — functional, not a security impact.

verdict.summary: No instantiated vulnerability: every array index fx into fdata is bounded by the loop condition (fx = rpmfiNext(fi)) >= 0 at all five iteration sites, and fdata is allocated from the same expression (fc = rpmfilesFC(files)) that bounds the iterators passed to rpmfiNext, so no in-domain attacker value reaches an out-of-bounds access. Archive error sentinels are caught by the explicit check 'if (!rc && fx < 0 && fx != RPMERR_ITER_END) rc = fx;'. Remaining issues (fc==0 allocation, *failedFile dereference, NULL payload for erase transactions, TOCTOU on filesystem operations inside not-shown callees) are speculative under the given code.

assumptions: rpmfiNext, when given an iterator constructed from 'files' (rpmfilesIter(files,...) / rpmfiNewArchiveReader(payload, files, ...)), returns an index in [0, rpmfilesFC(files)) or a negative sentinel; this is the standard iterator contract and matches the same-collection sizing of fdata.
xcalloc aborts the process on allocation failure rather than returning NULL.
failedFile is a valid non-NULL out-parameter per the calling convention of the psm layer.
limitations: xcalloc(fc, sizeof(*fdata)) with fc==0 relies on calloc(0,n) returning a unique non-NULL pointer (glibc behavior); on an allocator returning NULL for zero-size requests, the checked-allocation fatal path would abort on a valid zero-file package (denial of service at most, no corruption).

Filesystem TOCTOU/symlink race handling (suffix use, O_NOFOLLOW, rename-based commit) lives inside fsmMkfile/fsmCommit/fsmSetmeta, which are not shown; no race window can be instantiated from quoted statements here.

FA_TOUCH entries skip the 'fp->stage = FILE_UNPACK' assignment due to the early 'continue'; combined with the failure-erase branch 'fp->stage > FILE_NONE' this may remove a pre-existing file that was only touched during rollback — a semantics quirk whose impact depends on callee and filesystem state not shown.
rpmtePayload(te) may return NULL for erase-type transactions; Fclose/fdOp on a NULL FD_t would be a same-privilege crash at worst and is not attacker-triggerable corruption.

verdict.summary: chmd_read_headers performs fixed-length mspack_memcmp calls on a PMGL entry filename ('name') without verifying that name_len covers the compared ranges; a CHM file with a 2-byte '::' name near the end of a chunk drives reads up to ~105 bytes past the heap-allocated chunk buffer (out-of-bounds read).

evidence.reason: Fixed 31-byte compare at &name[2] with no guard that name_len >= 33; with name_len = 2 (allowed by line 195) and the entry near the chunk end, this reads past the chunk_size-byte heap allocation. Trigger: attacker-crafted CHM PMGL entry with name '::' positioned near end of chunk.

Worst-case instantiation of the same defect: reads name[33..104] (72 bytes) though name_len may be as small as 2 and no statement bounds the read to the chunk buffer; up to ~105 bytes past the allocation are consumed.

Origin of the tainted pointer: 'name' points into the attacker-supplied heap chunk, and the only name_len checks (line 188 entry-fit check, line 195 name_len<2 test) never establish that 105 bytes from name are readable.

assumptions: READ_ENCINT (macro not shown) is assumed to bound its reads against 'end' as in upstream libmspack; the OOB finding does not depend on this since the memcmps at lines 225-235 are unconditional once name_len >= 2.
pmgl_Entries is a small fixed offset (< 0x54-class constants), so &chunk[chm->chunk_size - 2] is in-bounds under the line 106 lower bound.
limitations: Line 95 'chm->sec0.offset = chm->dir_offset + (chm->chunk_size * chm->num_chunks)' can overflow 32-bit multiplication on version<3 files, but the resulting offset is consumed outside this function (seeks/extraction not shown), so no in-code impact is instantiated.
QuickRefSize checks at lines 173-180 only emit warnings; the value is never used as a memory bound in this code, so no OOB follows here.

verdict.summary: All attacker-controlled command-line values are consumed behind quoted guards: every argv[i+1]/argv[++i] use is preceded by CHECK_FOR_REQUIRED_ARGUMENT ('((i + 1) >= argc) || (!argv[i + 1])') with the correct >= operator and a NULL test; privileged options (-modulepath, -logfile) fail closed behind xf86PrivsElevated() and (-config, -configdir) behind xf86CheckPrivs before any state is set; -configure/-showopts reject the setuid case via 'getuid() != 0 && geteuid() == 0'; the -gamma value is range-checked with correct operators; strtol/sscanf inputs are NULL- and sentinel-checked. No reachable sink lacks a guard.

rpmPackageFilesInstall indexes fdata[fx] using the return of rpmfiNext() with only a lower-bound check (>= 0) and no upper-bound check against fc, the element count used to size fdata via xcalloc(fc, sizeof(*fdata)). For an added package, fi is an archive reader over the attacker-supplied cpio payload; a payload/header file-list mismatch can yield fx >= fc, so &fdata[fx] points out of bounds and the subsequent writes through fp (fp->action, fp->fpath, fp->stage, fsmMkfile) corrupt heap memory in the privileged install process.

evidence.reason: Root cause: out-of-bounds write. fc (line 10) sizes fdata (line 15) with exactly fc elements, but the only guard on fx is the lower-bound test '(fx = rpmfiNext(fi)) >= 0'; no statement checks fx < fc. Instantiated trigger: attacker-supplied .rpm with TR_ADDED whose payload (line 4/53 archive reader) yields fx = fc (one-past, e.g. fc=1, fx=1); the guard passes (1 >= 0), fp = &fdata[1] is past the allocation, and the loop writes through fp (fp->skip, fp->action, fp->fpath, fp->stage = FILE_UNPACK, fsmMkfile), corrupting heap memory.

Same missing guard at the first use of fdata: the header-driven iterator's return is consumed with only the >= 0 lower-bound check and no fx < fc upper bound before &fdata[fx]; any returned index >= fc indexes past the fc-element allocation and the loop body writes fp->action, fp->skip, fp->suffix, fp->fpath and fp->stage through the out-of-bounds pointer.

assumptions: The installed package (header file list and cpio payload) originates across a trust boundary, so header/payload-derived values (fc, file modes, link targets, iterator indices) are attacker-data.
rpmfiNext()'s producer is not shown in this code, so per the width-domain rule its return is treated as the full domain of int; only the sentinel lower bound (-1) is locally tested.
xcalloc aborts on allocation failure (rpm allocator semantics), so the fc==0/ENOMEM path is not a NULL-dereference risk.
limitations: If the caller passes failedFile == NULL, 'rc' paths executing *failedFile = xstrdup(fp->fpath) dereference NULL; this is a same-privilege crash with no corruption or bypass shown, and the caller's contract is not visible here.

At line 37 rc = rpmfiStat(fi, 1, &fp->sb) is overwritten at line 43 by rc = rpmpluginsCallFsmFilePre(...), so a stat failure can be masked and fp->sb may be uninitialized at later S_ISREG(fp->sb.st_mode) uses; whether rpmfiStat leaves sb fully/partially unset on failure is not characterizable from this code (CWE-457 candidate, impact link incomplete).

The later forward/backward loops (fsmSetmeta/fsmCommit/fsmRemove) repeat the &fdata[fx] pattern with the same one-sided >= 0 guard; they are treated as the same defect family reached only after the payload loop, not as independent findings.

Exact exploitability depends on the unshown archive-reader implementation returning an index >= fc on header/payload mismatch; per the full-domain rule this is assumed instantiable, which is why confidence is moderate-high rather than higher.

verdict.summary: jpc_pi_nextrpcl computes pi->prcno from attacker-controlled codestream geometry (prchind/prcvind from SIZ/COD/POC parameters) with no runtime bound; the only containment statement is assert(pi->prcno < pi->pirlvl->numprcs), which is compiled out in release builds (NDEBUG). The unchecked prcno indexes the numprcs-entry array pi->pirlvl->prclyrnos, giving an out-of-bounds read at line 87 and an attacker-scalable out-of-bounds write via ++(*prclyrno) at line 89.

evidence.reason: Origin: prcno is derived from prchind/prcvind, which are computed from attacker-controlled codestream values (x, xstart, prcwidthexpn, numhprcs) with no range validation against the precinct grid; a misaligned image offset yields prcno == numprcs or larger.

Missing-check site: this is the only statement bounding prcno, but assert is removed under NDEBUG and provides no runtime protection, so the bound required by the sink does not exist in any build used in production.

Sink: with the simulated trigger prcno = numprcs (one-past), prclyrnos[prcno] is past the numprcs-entry allocation; *prclyrno reads out of bounds and ++(*prclyrno) writes out of bounds — heap memory corruption driven by a crafted JPEG-2000 codestream.

assumptions: prclyrnos is allocated with numprcs entries, as its decode-side counterpart allocates per precinct (characterizable from the standard decoder semantics); the defect is the unbounded index, not the allocation.
Trigger values (xstart/xend, prcwidthexpn, numhprcs, numvprcs, POC fields) are attacker-instantiable per their declared int domains since no quoted validation constrains them in this code.
limitations: Secondary candidate: a negative pchg->compnostart or pchg->rlvlnostart (POC marker) passes the '< numcomps' / '< maxrlvls' loop conditions and, for negative rlvlno, passes the line-57 '>= numrlvls' check, giving pirlvls[negative] OOB reads at line 60; realizable unless unshown POC parsing rejects negatives.
If all hsamp/vsamp are zero (or numcomps == 0), pi->xstep/ystep stay 0 and lines 49/51 divide by zero — a crash-class robustness issue, superseded by the primary heap-overflow finding.
In debug builds the assert aborts (denial of service) before the OOB access; in standard release builds (NDEBUG) the OOB read/write is reachable.

verdict.summary: The only attacker-controlled value, len, is validated by 'if (len % ctx->blocksize) { ... return -1; }' before both decryption sinks, correctly rejecting any non-multiple-of-blocksize length in execution order; out-buffer sizing is a caller contract with no locally expressible check, and the unsupported-mode default arm fails closed. Remaining concerns (division by zero if blocksize==0, and decrypting with the ctx_encrypt fallback when ctx_decrypt is NULL) depend on unshown init-path state and produce no instantiated memory-safety or bypass impact in this code.

assumptions: ctx->blocksize, ctx->iv, and the algorithm context pointers are established by a successful cipher-init path (not shown) and ctx->blocksize > 0 there.
nettle cbc_decrypt/ECB primitives require length to be a multiple of block size and write exactly len bytes into out, reading exactly len bytes from in.
Out and in buffers are guaranteed by the caller to be at least len bytes; no out/in size parameter exists in this API, so no local check is expressible.
limitations: Speculative: 'len % ctx->blocksize' is a division by zero if ctx->blocksize were 0, but blocksize is set by the unshown init path and no statement here can produce 0; at worst a same-privilege crash.

Speculative: when ctx->ctx_decrypt is NULL the code decrypts using ctx->ctx_encrypt ('ctx->ctx_decrypt ? ctx->ctx_decrypt : ctx->ctx_encrypt'); whether this yields incorrect plaintext depends on the algorithm context layout in the unshown init code, and even then the impact is correctness (garbage plaintext with return 0), not a memory-safety or verification bypass shown in this code.
Cosmetic: the default arm's error message reports 'Unsupported cipher algorithm %d' using cipher->alg although the failure is an unsupported cipher mode; the arm still fails closed with return -1.

verdict.summary: All attacker-derived stream/packet fields (time_base, frame_rate_base, pts/dts/duration) flow only into av_rescale/av_frac_add and scalar assignments; these consume any int64 input with defined semantics and produce at worst corrupt timestamps. The only locally computed divisor pair is guarded by 'if (den && num)'. No memory access, copy, indexing, injection, authz, or resource-consumption sink consumes attacker data unsafely.

assumptions: av_rescale and av_frac_add exhibit standard FFmpeg semantics: they perform 64-bit-safe rescaling/accumulation, return a sentinel on zero denominator, and never write outside the AVFrac struct.
compute_frame_duration and get_audio_frame_size are consumed only through the quoted checks 'if (den && num)' and 'frame_size >= 0'.
limitations: Candidate C1: 'int num, den' are stack locals written only by the unshown callee compute_frame_duration; if that callee returns without setting them, 'if (den && num)' reads uninitialized values (CWE-457). Impact is limited to a garbage pkt->duration/timestamp skew in a same-privilege muxing process — no memory corruption, disclosure, bypass, or amplification — so it is a robustness issue, not a confirmed vulnerability; whether the callee initializes them cannot be verified from this code.

Candidate C2: st->time_base.num == 0 (attacker-controlled stream header) makes the av_rescale divisor zero; av_rescale's defined zero-denominator behavior absorbs this (no crash), but if the deployed version lacks that check this would be a division-related defect inside the callee.

Candidate C3: st->codec.frame_rate_base and st->time_base.den are unvalidated attacker header values fed to av_frac_add; worst case is an arbitrarily skewed pts fraction (functional timing corruption), no memory primitive.

verdict.summary: congratulate_user() passes an attacker-scaled size (18 + userName_size + 1) to snprintf instead of the actual buffer capacity (buffer_size = 30), which is never used. A command-line username of 13 or more bytes makes snprintf write past the end of the 30-byte stack buffer in main(), giving a scalable stack out-of-bounds write with attacker-chosen content.

evidence.reason: The size argument is computed from the attacker-controlled userName_size rather than buffer_size; with userName_size = 20 the call writes 38 bytes into the 30-byte buffer[30] declared in main(), overflowing it by 8 attacker-chosen bytes. The buffer_size parameter is never referenced in the function body, so no statement bounds the copy to the destination capacity.
Taint origin: strlen(argv[1]) feeds userName_size directly from an untrusted command-line argument with no length validation, enabling the oversized snprintf write at line 15.

verdict.summary: ChunkedDecode validates only the source span of each chunk (p + 2 + chunkLength > end) but never validates the destination offset reqPtr->chunkWriteOff before the memmove and the trailing NUL write; a chunkWriteOff outside the buffer (full size_t domain, producer not shown) yields an attacker-controlled out-of-bounds heap write.

evidence.reason: Root cause: writeBuffer is derived from reqPtr->chunkWriteOff, for which no bounds, range, clamp, or entry check exists anywhere in the function (mention sweep covers lines 39/41/42/43, which only use or update the field). The only bounds check, `if (p + 2 + chunkLength > end)` (line 33), constrains the source base p+2 — a different variable in the wrong unit for the destination. Trigger: chunkWriteOff = 0x10000 (or length), buffer "5\r\nhello", update=true → line 33 passes (p+2+5 == end) and memmove writes attacker-controlled chunk data past the Tcl_DString allocation, followed by a NUL byte at writeBuffer+chunkLength.

assumptions: Tcl_DString buffer is NUL-terminated at string[length], which bounds the strstr scan (Tcl invariant).
Pointer-overflow analysis assumes an LP64 layout (long/size_t 64-bit, heap below 2^47), so strtol-saturated LONG_MAX does not wrap the line 33 pointer sum.

reqPtr->chunkStartOff/chunkWriteOff are request-scoped fields whose initialization/reset code is not shown; per the full-domain rule any representable size_t value is treated as instantiable at the use.
limitations: If the unshown request setup provably resets chunkWriteOff to 0 (with chunkWriteOff <= chunkStartOff <= buffer length) before each chunked body, the simulated out-of-range trigger requires a stale offset from a reused request struct; the destination-side check is nonetheless absent in this code.

On 32-bit (ILP32) builds with the heap mapped above 0x80000000, an attacker-supplied chunk header saturating strtol to LONG_MAX (0x7fffffff) wraps the guard arithmetic `p + 2 + chunkLength > end` and permits a ~2GB memmove; this is platform-conditional and not triggerable on LP64.

When p + 2 + chunkLength == end, the decoder advances chunkStartOff by +4, virtually consuming a trailing CRLF that may not have arrived, and can return SOCK_READY with chunkStartOff = length + 2 — a pipelined-request desync (smuggling-adjacent); the downstream driver behavior is not shown.
strtol accepts junk/trailer lines as length 0 (and hex strings with a leading '-' are rejected only by the line 26 negative check); this is parsing leniency, not memory corruption.

verdict.summary: The only attacker-controlled input, argv[1], is rendered through a size-matched snprintf with a compile-time format literal into a 30-byte stack buffer; snprintf caps writes at 30 bytes and guarantees NUL termination, so the subsequent printf("%s", buffer) is safe. No injection, overflow, or truncation-based security impact exists.

assumptions: argv strings are NUL-terminated per the C standard main contract, which the %s consumption in snprintf and strlen rely on.
limitations: The parameter userName_size is accepted but never used; truncation of very long usernames occurs by design (output only, no security impact).

If congratulate_user were reused with a caller passing buffer_size <= 0, snprintf would write nothing; no such caller exists in this code, and snprintf with size 0 performs no write, so even that general-domain case is not a memory-safety defect.

verdict.summary: virgl_cmd_get_capset decodes the guest-controlled capset_version (VIRTIO_GPU_FILL_CMD) but never validates it against the host renderer's max_ver before passing it to virgl_renderer_fill_caps, while the destination buffer is allocated with the max_size returned by virgl_renderer_get_cap_set (i.e., sized for versions up to max_ver). A guest sending a supported capset_id with capset_version > max_ver reaches fill_caps with a version selecting a larger data layout than the allocated buffer, producing a guest-triggered out-of-bounds write in the host process. The only validation present, `if (!max_size)`, does not bound the version; the upstream fix adds `|| max_ver < gc.capset_version`.

evidence.reason: Unvalidated use: gc.capset_version is raw guest data (u32) passed to the host-side fill routine, whose output size depends on the version, while resp was sized at line 14 from max_size obtained for versions up to max_ver. No statement anywhere bounds capset_version; trigger: guest GET_CAPSET with capset_id=1, capset_version=2 while max_ver=1, max_size=v1 size → host OOB write past the g_malloc'd buffer. Missing guard: `max_ver < gc.capset_version` in the line-10 check.
Taint origin: the guest-supplied control command is decoded into gc here, making gc.capset_version (and gc.capset_id) attacker-controlled across the trust boundary with the full u32 domain.

assumptions: VIRTIO_GPU_FILL_CMD populates gc from the guest-submitted virtqueue command, making its fields attacker-data (standard virtio-gpu semantics).

virgl_renderer_fill_caps sizes the caps data it writes according to the version argument (the standard virglrenderer contract); the buffer at resp->capset_data is only max_size bytes, valid for versions <= max_ver.
limitations: The actual overwrite length depends on virgl_renderer_fill_caps behavior (not shown); the defect confirmed here is the absence of the version bound at the call site, matching the upstream fix that adds `max_ver < gc.capset_version`.
Integer-overflow of sizeof(*resp)+max_size would require max_size near 2^32 from the host renderer, not quotable from this code — speculative.
g_malloc failure is not NULL-tested, but g_malloc aborts on OOM by design (standard QEMU semantics), so no NULL-deref candidate stands.

verdict.summary: This JNI wrapper passes the attacker-domain jint cpIndex and the constantPoolOop reference verbatim to getFieldAt with no local bounds or NULL check. The only quoted statement is the call; any actual indexing/dereference occurs inside the not-shown callee getFieldAt, whose semantics are neither quoted nor characterizable as a standard function, so no impact link can be instantiated in this code. The defect, if any, must be judged where the index is consumed.

assumptions: getFieldAt(env, constantPoolOop, cpIndex, flags) is a callee whose implementation is not shown and is not a standard library function with characterizable sentinel/indexing semantics; no quoted contract bounds cpIndex.
The JNI entry point is reachable only from Java code via sun.reflect.ConstantPool; per discipline 4 the full jint domain of cpIndex is treated as instantiable.
limitations: Candidate (speculative, not confirmed): cpIndex is passed unchecked (no `cpIndex >= 0 && cpIndex < constantPoolCount` test, no NULL test on constantPoolOop anywhere in the given code) into getFieldAt. If the unshown getFieldAt indexes the constant pool without its own bounds check, an out-of-range cpIndex (e.g. -1 or 2^31-1) yields an out-of-bounds read or NULL dereference in a JVM-privileged process — that would be CWE-125/CWE-476 at the callee's indexing site, but the defect and its guard both live outside this snippet and cannot be adjudicated here.
J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_NO_THROW_ON_FAIL indicates the resolve path is not expected to throw; any error/exception handling on that path is not shown and was not evaluated.

verdict.summary: The CC comment handler consumes attacker-shaped command input, but the only memory-safety-sensitive site (case '+'/' ') allocates from strlen(comment)+strlen(newcomment)+2 while appending only strings that provably cannot exceed those lengths: nc is derived from newcomment via r_str_unescape and r_str_ansi_strip, both of which only shrink, and malloc/NULL/comment sentinels are tested in execution order. All other sinks (r_str_newf with fixed formats, strchr/strdup paths, sdb_decode, r_str_between, r_cons_printf) carry NULL or bounds guards on every path.

assumptions: r_str_unescape and r_str_ansi_strip operate in place and only shrink the string (each escape sequence consumes >=2 source bytes and emits <=1 byte); under this standard semantics the allocation strlen(comment)+strlen(newcomment)+2 is always sufficient for strcpy(comment)+strcat(" ")+strcat(nc).
input is a NUL-terminated command string; reads of input[2] and input[3] are therefore always within the buffer (input[3] is read only when input[2] is non-NUL).
limitations: If strdup(newcomment) returns NULL (allocation failure), r_str_unescape/r_str_ansi_strip and the free path would dereference NULL — same-privilege crash robustness issue only, requires OOM precondition.

nc (user comment text) is embedded into undo/redo command strings (r_str_newf("CC %s@0x%08"PFMT64x, nc, addr)); if those strings are later re-executed by undo machinery not shown here and comments can originate from untrusted project files, command injection at replay would be possible — impact link outside this code, not instantiated.

The loop 'for (i = 0; i < bb->size; i++)' compares int i against the block size; a pathologically huge bb->size from a parsed binary could cause long iteration, but no wrap or OOB is quotable from the given statements.

verdict.summary: The JNI entry point passes raw attacker-reachable jint cpIndex and jobject constantPoolOop unchecked into getFieldAt, but the only memory-affecting use of those values occurs entirely inside the not-shown callee, whose validation behavior is neither quoted nor characterizable as a standard function; no impact chain is instantiated within this code, so no defect is provable here.

assumptions: getFieldAt(env, constantPoolOop, cpIndex, flag) is an internal helper whose body is not shown and is not a standard library function, so its handling of cpIndex and constantPoolOop cannot be characterized per discipline 3.
J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_NO_CLASS_LOAD is an internal trusted constant, not attacker-influenced.
limitations: Candidate: cpIndex (full jint domain, including negative and out-of-pool values) and constantPoolOop (possibly NULL) are passed to getFieldAt without any local range or NULL check. If getFieldAt indexes the constant pool without validating cpIndex, this call site conveys an out-of-domain index to the vulnerable use (potential CWE-125/787 or CWE-476). This could not be confirmed because the harmful use is entirely inside the unshown callee and no quoted contract bounds cpIndex; per STEP 4 the impact link is not instantiated in this code.

If a caller in the same package/VM is considered fully trusted (JNI methods of sun.reflect.ConstantPool are internal JDK plumbing), the attack surface narrows further; this code provides no basis for that judgment either way.

verdict.summary: All array indexing in compand_drain is internally consistent: the output frame is allocated with exactly FFMIN(2048, s->delay_count) samples matching the write loop bound, ff_get_audio_buffer fails on non-positive nb_samples (guarded by the quoted 'if (!frame) return AVERROR(ENOMEM)'), and the read index is confined to [0, delay_samples-1] by the MOD wrap (verified at both bounds for delay_samples >= 1); the subtraction s->delay_count -= frame->nb_samples cannot underflow. The only harmful states (delay_samples <= 0 with delay_count > 0, NULL delay_frame, out-of-range delay_index, channel-count mismatch) require the unshown sibling functions (config_output/activate/filter_frame) to violate invariants this code never produces, so they are speculative, not instantiated.

No attacker-controlled value reaches any sink in this exit handler. All consumed data is internal child-process state or privileged-local environment; the respawn limit is checked at its use, callee returns are branched on, and all log calls use literal format strings with constant daemon names. The realistic failure modes (stale IPC endpoint causing pcmk_child_active to report a dead daemon as alive, or a NULL child pointer from an unseen caller) cannot be instantiated from the given code.

assumptions: child points to a valid pcmk_child_t; this is a static helper whose callers are not shown and no statement in this code can produce NULL.
child->name and child->endpoint are fixed daemon identifier strings, not attacker-supplied content.
PCMK_fail_fast is set in the daemon's environment by the local administrator, not by a remote party.
limitations: If pcmk_child_active() can return 1 based on a stale IPC socket, a crashed daemon is marked active_before_startup = TRUE and never respawned unless the scheduled check_active_before_startup_processes callback repairs it; that behavior (and the callback) is not shown, so the impact is not instantiated here.
A NULL child argument would crash the same-privilege process; caller validation is not visible in this snippet.
The comparison 'respawn_count > MAX_RESPAWN' permits one respawn at exactly the limit before disabling; this is a policy off-by-one with no security consequence in this code.

verdict.summary: The exported function hash_passwords indexes passwords[i] (and usernames is paired with it) using the caller-supplied count as the sole loop bound, with no check that passwords.size() >= count; std::vector::operator[] is unchecked, so any caller passing count larger than the vector size reads out of bounds, including passing the OOB length to PKCS5_PBKDF2_HMAC.

The salt's security function (per-record uniqueness/unpredictability) is entirely defeated.

evidence.reason: Root cause: predictable salt (CWE-760). The intended entropy source (RAND_bytes) exists only as comments (lines 27-30) and is never executed; this memset writes a constant all-zero salt for every record before PKCS5_PBKDF2_HMAC consumes it (line 35) and it is printed/stored per record. Instantiated trigger: any run of the program, e.g. two users with args u1 p1 u2 p2 — both records receive salt 0x00*32, so an attacker precomputes one dictionary for that salt and matches all stored hashes.

assumptions: The hashed passwords and salts returned by hash_passwords are intended for storage/verification in a database (stated in the function's documentation comment), so the constant salt is a security-relevant stored value, not merely cosmetic output.
Command-line argv is the attacker-data trust boundary for password content; the password content itself is passed to PBKDF2 correctly (length-aware, NUL bytes safe).

The usernames parameter is accepted but never used, so hashed records are not bound to usernames; treated as functional, not a direct security impact in this code.
If count were negative, hashed_passwords(count) would be empty and the loop would not execute (i < count fails immediately), so no out-of-bounds access results.
10000 PBKDF2 iterations is below modern OWASP recommendations (~600k for PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA-256) but meets the stated specification; recorded as hardening note, not a defect.

The fixed-index writes outbuf[0]/outbuf[1] are constant and in-bounds for any message buffer. Violations would require the external state machine (not shown) to set outpos > outlen or outlen > sizeof(outbuf), which this code cannot instantiate.

side_in_cb sizes the message read buffer from g_dbus_message_bytes_needed(), whose result is derived from attacker-controlled D-Bus header fields (uint32 body_len), and the only check, `if (required < 0)`, does not bound the upper end. A sandboxed app that has completed the auth handshake can send a 16-byte header declaring body_len = 0xFFFFFFFF, causing buffer_new() to g_malloc ~4 GB per message — attacker-scalable memory exhaustion (or g_malloc abort) of the host-level proxy process.

evidence.reason: Taint origin and missing guard: `required` is computed from the attacker-controlled D-Bus header (body_len is a uint32 at header offset 4, so required can reach 16 + 0xFFFFFFFF ≈ 4.29 GB), but the only validation rejects just the negative/error direction — no upper bound on the allocation size exists anywhere between this check and the allocation.

Sink: buffer_new() allocates a buffer of `required` bytes. Trigger: a client-side (sandboxed app) peer completes auth (client->authenticated set at line 69), then sends a 16-byte header with body_len = 0xFFFFFFFF; required = 4294967312 passes `required < 0` and is passed unchecked as the allocation size, yielding a ~4 GB g_malloc per message, repeatable for unbounded memory exhaustion or g_malloc abort.

assumptions: g_dbus_message_bytes_needed follows standard GLib semantics: it returns 16 + align8(fields_len) + body_len for a complete 16-byte header and does not enforce a maximum message size (only an internal G_MAXSSIZE overflow check).

The client side of the proxy is the untrusted sandboxed application across the sandbox trust boundary; completing the D-Bus auth handshake (which the attacker itself controls) is sufficient to reach the authenticated header-processing path.
header_buffer is a fixed 16-byte buffer, so the line-81 call always receives a complete GDBus fixed header containing the attacker-supplied body_len and fields_len fields.
limitations: find_auth_end is not shown; if it could return a value greater than buffer->pos, `extra_data = buffer->pos - buffer->size` (line 49) would underflow to a huge gsize and g_bytes_new at line 54 would read out of bounds — not confirmable from the given code, so not part of the verdict.

Whether g_malloc ultimately aborts or the host OOM-kills the proxy depends on runtime memory pressure; either outcome is denial of service of the host-level proxy process, and no memory-corruption primitive is claimed.
The `required == 16` edge case (a message exactly the size of the fixed header) may be a forwarding bug, but its impact within the shown code is at most functional and was not pursued.

verdict.summary: No instantiated vulnerability. All sinks carry quoted, correctly-positioned guards: 'if (comma == NULL) { errno = EINVAL; return NULL; }' handles the strchr miss; 'comma - url >= 7' exactly bounds the &comma[-7] read (index 7 reads url[0], index 6 is short-circuited); both malloc results are NULL-checked before the decoders write ('if (buffer == NULL) return NULL;'); and 'if (fp == NULL) { free(buffer); return NULL; }' precedes the only fp dereference. Buffer sizes derive from the same expressions that bound the paired decode (base64: hts_base64_decoded_length(strlen(data)); percent: strlen(data)+1, and percent decoding strictly shrinks input).

assumptions: hts_decode_base64 writes at most hts_base64_decoded_length(strlen(data)) bytes into buffer and sets *length, per the paired htslib API the shown allocation mirrors; hts_decode_percent likewise decodes in place without expansion and sets *length.
malloc(0) behavior is handled by the quoted NULL checks and a zero-length decode writes nothing.
limitations: Speculative: a heap overflow in the base64 branch (candidate C3) could exist only if hts_base64_decoded_length underestimates the output of hts_decode_base64 for some input (e.g., decoding continuing past '=' padding). The callee internals are not shown and no statement in this code instantiates such a value, so this cannot be confirmed from the given code.

The else-branch buffer is not explicitly NUL-terminated here; it is passed as a fixed-size (buffer, length, size) triple to hfile_init_fixed, which is consistent, but if a downstream consumer treated it as a C string an unterminated-buffer issue would arise outside this code.
The mode-parameter check permits any string containing 'r' (e.g. 'r+w'); no write support exists, but that is a functional limitation, not a security defect in this code.

verdict.summary: controller::bookmark builds a shell command line from attacker-controlled feed fields (title, description, feed_title) with only the STFL UI-escaper stfl::quote applied — no shell encoding — and executes it via /bin/sh -c, enabling shell metacharacter injection (e.g. $(cmd), backticks) and arbitrary command execution when the user bookmarks an attacker-supplied article. The url field is guarded by single-quote wrapping plus replace_all(url, "'", "%27"), but the three other feed fields are interpolated unquoted.

evidence.reason: Sink: cmdline is executed through /bin/sh -c, so any shell metacharacter surviving in it performs command substitution/redirection. Trigger: feed title set to "$(id)" by the feed author; the shell runs the substitution during bookmarking.

evidence.snippet:
std::string cmdline = strprintf::fmt("%s '%s' %s %s %s",
			                               bookmark_cmd,
			                               utils::replace_all(url,"'", "%27"),
			                               quote_empty(stfl::quote(title)),
evidence.reason: Origin: cmdline is assembled by string interpolation. The url is shell-safe (single-quoted with ' stripped by replace_all), but title/description/feed_title are passed through stfl::quote — an STFL UI-syntax escaper, not a shell escaper — and interpolated as bare arguments, so $(), backticks, and other shell metacharacters in feed-supplied metadata reach the shell unencoded.

assumptions: url/title/description/feed_title derive from feed content and thus cross a trust boundary; bookmark-cmd and bookmark-interactive are local user configuration and treated as trusted for this analysis.
The code runs when the user invokes bookmarking with bookmark-cmd configured (line 9 guard), which is the intended use of this feature.
limitations: stfl::quote's implementation is not shown; the analysis does not rely on its exact behavior — no quoted statement in this code shell-encodes title/description/feed_title, and the historical stfl::quote escapes only STFL/UI characters, leaving $() and backticks intact.
Execution also occurs on the interactive path via utils::run_interactively(cmdline, ...) (line 22), same root cause.
Impact is arbitrary command execution as the user running the reader; no privilege escalation beyond the user's own shell is claimed.

verdict.summary: controller::bookmark builds a debug log line from attacker-controlled feed fields (url, title, description, feed_title) after escaping only single quotes (utils::replace_all(x, "'", "%27")), leaving newlines and carriage returns intact. A feed publisher can embed newline characters in an item title/URL, so the LOG statement at line 17 emits forged log entries. The adjacent shell-execution sinks (/bin/sh -c at lines 22/29) are NOT injectable because the quoted %27 replacement provably keeps every field inside single quotes, the only sh escape context.

evidence.reason: Log-line sink: cmdline embeds raw attacker feed content. Only single quotes were replaced; a title like "x\nSep 21 26: login failed for admin" flows verbatim into the log, forging log entries (CWE-117). No statement encodes newlines.

evidence.snippet:
std::string cmdline = strprintf::fmt("%s '%s' '%s' '%s' '%s'",
		                                       bookmark_cmd,
		                                       utils::replace_all(url,"'", "%27"),
		                                       utils::replace_all(title,"'", "%27"),
		                                       utils::replace_all(description,"'", "%27"),
		                                       utils::replace_all(feed_title,"'", "%27"));
evidence.reason: Taint origin: the only validation applied to the attacker-controlled feed fields is replacement of the single-quote character. Newline/CR pass through unmodified, which is sufficient for the shell sinks (single-quote context makes them literal) but not for the log sink at line 17.

assumptions: url, title, description, feed_title originate from parsed feed content supplied by a remote publisher (trust-boundary crossing), consistent with their use as feed item fields.
LOG at debug level writes the formatted string to a persistent log file or stderr; the call itself is quoted as the construction site of the forged line.
limitations: Command injection (CWE-78) into /bin/sh -c was considered and dismissed on a quoted guard: utils::replace_all(x, "'", "%27") removes every single quote from all four fields before interpolation, and within unbroken single quotes no POSIX sh metacharacter (newline, $, backtick, &, |) is interpreted. bookmark_cmd is interpolated unescaped but is local user configuration, not attacker data.
No format-string defect: cmdline is passed as a %s argument to strprintf::fmt and LOG, never as the format string.
Impact limited to debug-level log forging (low severity); whether the debug log is enabled is a deployment property, not required by the output-construction rule.

verdict.summary: hfile_mem_get_buffer computes the output length with reversed operand order: `file->buffer - file->limit` is the negative of the buffer capacity (base minus end), and storing that negative ptrdiff_t into size_t wraps to a near-SIZE_MAX value, so every caller that requested the buffer size receives a length far beyond the allocation, enabling out-of-bounds reads/copies in any size-based consumer of the returned buffer.

evidence.reason: Reversed pointer subtraction: buffer is the allocation base and limit the allocation end, so the difference is -(capacity); assignment to size_t wraps to 2^64 - capacity. Simulated: buffer=B, limit=B+N (N>0) → *length = 2^64 - N while only N bytes are allocated. No statement in the code bounds or corrects this value (line 2 checks backend identity, line 7 checks only the output pointer for NULL), so the function's own length output is out-of-domain and misreports the buffer size to every caller.

assumptions: hFILE layout follows htslib semantics: `buffer` is the start of the allocated backing store and `limit` its end (limit >= buffer), so `file->buffer - file->limit` is always <= 0 for any valid mem-backed file; no statement in this code contradicts this.
`length` may be NULL; line 7 (`if (length)`) correctly guards that case but does not constrain the stored value.
limitations: The out-of-bounds read itself occurs in callers of hfile_mem_get_buffer, which are not shown; the defect confirmed here is the wrapped (underflowed) length value produced by line 8, which is out-of-domain for the advertised buffer size regardless of consumer.

A NULL `file` argument dereferences at line 2 (`file->backend`), but that is a same-privilege crash with no corruption, disclosure, bypass, or amplification — a robustness issue, not a verdict-driving vulnerability.

verdict.summary: The logout URL hostname validation is skipped when apr_uri_parse yields a NULL hostname, so an attacker-supplied logout URL such as 'https:/evil.com' (which browsers normalize to https://evil.com) bypasses the mutual-substring host check and is embedded, escaped, as post_logout_redirect_uri in the end-session redirect, producing an open redirect to an attacker-controlled host.

evidence.reason: The hostname-match validation is conjunctively gated on uri.hostname != NULL; for attacker input like 'https:/evil.com' apr_uri_parse succeeds with hostname == NULL, so the whole check is skipped and the unvalidated attacker URL flows into the post_logout_redirect_uri redirect sink at lines 77-80/87. The missing guard is rejection of hostname-NULL URLs.
Origin of the attacker-controlled taint: the logout request parameter is read directly from the HTTP request and later used as the redirect target.

assumptions: oidc_is_front_channel_logout / oidc_is_back_channel_logout (lines 11/13) do not match arbitrary logout URLs; their bodies are not shown and they cannot serve as guards either way.

The OP end_session_endpoint honors the standard post_logout_redirect_uri parameter with a browser redirect, and browsers normalize scheme URLs with a single slash (e.g. 'https:/evil.com') to the authority form — standard OIDC/URL-spec semantics characterizable outside this code.
limitations: Log forging (CWE-117): the raw attacker url is written to logs at line 9 and via the hostname-mismatch error at lines 42-45 before the CR/LF check at line 53; whether oidc_debug/oidc_error escape newlines is not shown, so impact is not instantiated here.
oidc_debug at line 9 passes a possibly-NULL url to a %s format; at worst a same-privilege crash, not a security impact.
c_host returned by oidc_get_current_url_host is assumed non-NULL; a NULL there would be a crash, not the primary defect.

verdict.summary: In the replacement-copy loop of _php_mb_regex_ereg_replace_exec, fwd is computed from the multibyte lead byte without clamping to the remaining bytes of the attacker-supplied replacement string, so out_buf.append(p, fwd) on the final truncated multibyte character reads and returns up to 3 bytes past the end of the replacement buffer (out-of-bounds read / heap info leak into output).

evidence.reason: Sink: copies fwd bytes from p with no check that i+fwd <= replacement.size(). Trigger: replacement ending in a truncated multibyte char (e.g. "a\xF0" with UTF-8 encoding); at i=1 fwd=4 but only 1 byte remains, so append reads 3 bytes past the string data and appends them to the returned output.
Origin of the tainted length: fwd is derived from the attacker-controlled final lead byte of replacement (up to 4 for UTF-8) and is never clamped to replacement.size() - i before use.

assumptions: php_mb_mbchar_bytes_ex returns the encoding's declared character byte length from the lead byte at p (up to 4), and StringBuffer::append copies exactly len bytes — standard-function semantics.
This function is the backend of a userland PHP API (mb_ereg_replace/mbregex), so all parameters are attacker-controlled across a trust boundary.
limitations: Candidate (b): with a pattern matching empty at end-of-string, pos becomes string_lim+1 and is passed as start (> end) to onig_search (lines 64-65, 107-114); whether onig_search reads OOB or returns an error for start>end depends on unshown Oniguruma internals, so impact is speculative here.
Candidate (c): int i can overflow only for a replacement >= 2GB; after wrap the (size_t)i comparison exceeds replacement.size() and the loop exits, so no harmful use is instantiated.
regs = onig_region_new() is not NULL-checked; worst case is a same-privilege crash, a robustness issue only.

The overread is bounded by max multibyte width minus 1 (up to 3 bytes for UTF-8) and stays within the heap allocation if spare capacity follows the string data; disclosure impact depends on allocator layout.

verdict.summary: Unbounded copies of attacker-supplied command-line strings into fixed-size stack buffers: sscanf("%s") without a field width into char dr[10] (four sites) and strcpy() of optarg/argv[optind] into 255-byte buffers, causing stack buffer overflows with attacker-controlled data (classic CWE-120).

evidence.reason: Root cause: sscanf format "%s" has no field-width limit, copying the entire attacker-supplied option string into the 10-byte stack buffer dr. Trigger: `-s` (also -f, -b, -l) with an argument longer than 9 bytes (e.g. 64 'A's) writes past dr[10]; the `< 1` check only tests the parse result after the overflowed write and no length guard exists on any path. The same defect repeats at lines 94, 108, and 122.

Root cause: unbounded strcpy of the positional command-line argument into the 255-byte stack buffer aacFileName. Trigger: a positional argument longer than 254 bytes overflows the buffer; the only related check, `(argc - optind) < 1` (line 181), verifies the argument exists but never its length. Same pattern for strcpy(audioFileName, optarg) at line 69 and strcpy(adtsFileName, optarg) at line 76.

assumptions: getopt_long sets optarg to raw unmodified argv content (standard libc semantics), so option strings are attacker-controlled with no length limit.
The overflow targets are stack buffers (declared as local arrays), so overwriting adjacent locals/control data is a memory-corruption primitive.
limitations: fread(header, 1, 8, hMP4File) at the file-open block has no return check; if fewer than 8 bytes are read, header[4..7] are compared uninitialized (CWE-457) — robustness-grade, not promoted.
length/dec_length division can divide by zero if clock elapsed time is 0 — same-privilege crash, robustness only.
Values parsed with atoi after an overly long string corrupt the stack before validation (showHelp) can act; showHelp path does not prevent the already-committed overflow.

Severity assumes a context where untrusted parties control the command line (e.g. scripts wrapping this decoder over untrusted input); a purely interactive same-user CLI lowers practical exploitability but the code-level defect remains.

verdict.summary: qcrypto_cipher_decrypt passes the attacker-supplied size parameter `len` directly into block-cipher decryption (ctx->alg_decrypt for ECB, cbc_decrypt for CBC) without any check that len is a multiple of the cipher's block size. The mention sweep shows len is touched only at its declaration and at the two sink calls; no alignment, range, or size guard exists anywhere in the function, while the default arm rejects only unsupported modes. An out-of-domain length reaches the nettle primitives, causing host-process abort (assert) or partial/misaligned buffer processing in the higher-privileged QEMU process; upstream QEMU's twin carries exactly the removed guard `if (len % ctx->blocksize) { error_setg(...); return -1; }`.

evidence.snippet:
ctx->alg_decrypt(ctx->ctx_decrypt ? ctx->ctx_decrypt : ctx->ctx_encrypt,
                         len, out, in);
evidence.reason: Unvalidated use of attacker-data size `len`: the parameter is passed raw into the block-cipher decrypt primitive with no preceding `len % blocksize` check anywhere in the function (the identical CBC sink at lines 14-16 has the same defect). Trigger: any caller-supplied len not a multiple of the cipher block size (e.g. 137 for AES-256), representable in size_t, reaches this call and is handed to a whole-block cipher operation whose input domain is block-aligned lengths only.

assumptions: ctx->alg_decrypt, ctx->niv, ctx->iv and ctx->ctx_* are initialized by the cipher-creation code (not shown) to values matching cipher->alg/mode; only `len`, `in`, and `out` are treated as attacker-data per discipline 4.

Nettle block-cipher semantics per discipline 3: block primitives operate on whole blocks and abort (assert) or ignore trailing bytes for unaligned lengths; exact in-callee behavior is standard-function semantics, not quoted code.
limitations: Full out-of-bounds write is not provable from this code alone because the sizes of the `in`/`out` buffers are not parameters of this function; the concrete impact instantiated here is out-of-domain length consumption (host-process abort / partial decrypt) in a higher-privileged process, i.e., at least denial of service.
Line 19-20 prints `cipher->alg` while the switch tests `cipher->mode` — wrong variable in the diagnostic message; cosmetic/robustness only, not a fail-open path since the error arm still returns -1.
Reachability of an unaligned len from a specific QEMU caller (e.g., qcow2/LUKS block layer) is not shown; the defect is judged at this exported API's intake point per discipline 4.

verdict.summary: All attacker-reachable memory sinks are guarded: the per-iteration index clamp 'if (i >= (bsize - 32)) { i = 0; }' executes before every buf+i access and provably keeps i in [0, bsize-33] even after the chk_constraint loop clobbers i, matching the exact 'malloc (bsize)'/'r_io_read_at (..., bsize)' pairing; prev_type stays NUL-terminated because strncpy is bounded to sizeof(prev_type)-1 (writing at most indices 0..254) over the {0}-initialized 256-byte array; all callee sentinels (hc, buf, _pc, r, Cc, rt, rr, fcn_call, flag, f, mop, next_op, var, lvar, regitem, cur_dest) are NULL-checked before first use. Remaining candidates (r_read_ble with large aop.refptr, prev_dest sdb dangle, fcn->ninstr * 0xf overflow, early-return leaks) could not be instantiated without unshown callee behavior.

assumptions: r_read_ble is a width-dispatch helper (8/16/32/64-bit arms with a 64-bit default) that reads at most 8 bytes for any bits argument; the code contains no local bound on aop.refptr, so this callee semantics is what keeps 'r_read_ble (buf, core->print->big_endian, aop.refptr * 8)' inside the 256-byte stack buffer.
r_anal_op respects the length argument (bsize - i) and never decodes beyond it; r_core_anal_op may return NULL and every such return is NULL-checked here.
r_anal_block_contains and r_anal_op_free handle a NULL argument (standard radare2 sentinel behavior); sdb_const_get returns NULL on a miss and its return is guarded here.
get_src_regname(core, addr, dst, size) honors the passed size and NUL-terminates dst (callee not shown; size parameter is the quoted contract surface).
limitations: Candidate C3 (stack OOB read, CWE-125): 'ut64 ptr = r_read_ble (buf, core->print->big_endian, aop.refptr * 8)' has no local bound on aop.refptr; dismissed only because r_read_ble's width dispatch reads at most 8 bytes. If a deployed r_read_ble instead reads bits/8 bytes for arbitrary bits, this becomes a real OOB read — unprovable from the code given.

Candidate C4 (dangling read): 'prev_dest = sdb_const_get (trace, query, 0)' holds a pointer into the sdb across iterations while 'sdb_num_set' and 'r_core_esil_step' mutate the same database; a use-after-free would require the same key's value to be replaced in between — depends on ESIL/sdb internals not shown.
Candidate C5 (CWE-190): 'ht_pp_new_size (fcn->ninstr * 0xf, ...)' can overflow int when fcn->ninstr exceeds ~143M; no quoted producer can reach that scale within this run's analysis.

The chk_constraint loop 'for (i = 0; i < MAX_INSTR ; i++)' reuses the outer buffer index i, which desynchronizes buf+i from addr when i stays below bsize-32 (large blocksize) — the decode window remains in-bounds, so this is a functional misanalysis (wrong type propagation), not a memory-safety defect.

The early returns 'if (!_pc) { free (buf); return; }' and 'if (!r) { free (buf); return; }' leak the RConfigHold and skip anal_emul_restore — a resource leak with no corruption, bypass, or attacker-scalable amplification.

The code is an exported API entry point (R_API) whose fcn and its fields are attacker-derived from the parsed binary; reachability of the analysis pass by an untrusted file is assumed, as all findings were evaluated under that trust boundary.

verdict.summary: Guest-controlled gc.capset_version is passed unvalidated to virgl_renderer_fill_caps, which fills caps into resp->capset_data, a heap buffer sized only by max_size queried from gc.capset_id. The code fetches max_ver (the upper bound on valid versions) but never compares it against gc.capset_version, so a guest requesting an out-of-range version can drive a heap out-of-bounds write in the host QEMU process.

evidence.reason: Sink: the guest-controlled capset_version is passed raw into a memory-filling callee while the destination resp->capset_data was sized at line 14 from max_size (queried for capset_id only). No statement anywhere in the code compares gc.capset_version to max_ver or otherwise bounds it, so an out-of-range version (e.g., version 2 when the host reports max_ver 1 and max_size = v1 caps size) reaches the fill call and writes past the allocation — heap out-of-bounds write triggered by a guest command.
Origin of taint: the guest-supplied virtqueue command populates gc, including capset_id and capset_version (each 32-bit, full domain instantiable by the guest).

The code obtains max_ver — the maximum valid capset version for this capset_id, the exact value a guard needs — and then never reads it; the buffer is sized solely by max_size. This is the one-line guard whose absence is the defect: a check like 'if (gc.capset_version > max_ver) return error;' placed after this call would prevent the out-of-range version from reaching virgl_renderer_fill_caps.

assumptions: virgl_renderer_fill_caps writes the caps layout corresponding to the requested capset_version into the caller buffer (the renderer protocol's documented semantics; max_ver/max_size returned by virgl_renderer_get_cap_set describe the valid version range and size), so a version above max_ver can cause a write larger than max_size.
VIRTIO_GPU_FILL_CMD reads the guest-supplied command payload, making gc.capset_id and gc.capset_version attacker-data from the guest VM (trust boundary: guest to host QEMU process).
limitations: Uninitialized max_ver/max_size (line 6) if virgl_renderer_get_cap_set fails to set its output arguments on an unknown capset_id would give an uninitialized stack value controlling allocation and response size; however, the only instantiable miss sentinel (0) is caught by 'if (!max_size)' at line 10, and producing nonzero garbage requires unshown callee behavior, so this candidate is speculative.

The concrete write length inside virgl_renderer_fill_caps is not shown; the confirmed defect is the call site passing an unvalidated, out-of-domain guest version into a memory-fill of a fixed-size buffer, with no quoted guard anywhere in this code bounding it.
No integer overflow exists in 'sizeof(*resp) + max_size' since sizeof yields 64-bit size_t and max_size is u32; g_malloc0 aborts on failure rather than returning NULL.

verdict.summary: Four occurrences of `sscanf(optarg, "%s", dr)` copy an unbounded attacker-supplied command-line option argument into a 10-byte stack buffer `char dr[10]` with no field-width bound (`%9s`) or length check anywhere, producing a stack out-of-bounds write with attacker-controlled content and length.

evidence.reason: Root cause: unbounded `%s` copies attacker-controlled optarg of arbitrary length into the 10-byte stack buffer dr. Trigger: `-s 0123456789ABCDEF` writes 17 bytes into 10. The only nearby statement mentioning optarg (`if (optarg)`) is a NULL check, not a length check, and the sscanf return comparison executes after the overflowing copy.
Same unbounded-copy defect for the -f option: any option string longer than 9 chars overflows dr before the conversion-count check runs.
Same unbounded-copy defect for the -b option; the subsequent range validation of outputFormat (lines 125-126) validates the parsed value, not the copy length, so it is not a guard for the overflow.
Same unbounded-copy defect for the -l option; the enumerated-object-type check (lines 139-142) validates object_type, not the copy length, and runs after the stack write.

assumptions: sscanf with `%s` copies until whitespace/NUL with no bound, per standard semantics; the overflow therefore reaches arbitrarily far past dr with attacker-chosen bytes.
The -o/-a filename handling is safe: `malloc(sizeof(char) * (strlen(optarg) + 1))` sizes the buffer from the same expression as the `strcpy`, and the NULL-return sentinel is checked before use.
format is safely bounded before `file_ext[format]` indexing: `if ((format < 1) || (format > 2)) showHelp = 1;` plus the `usage(); return 1;` early exit on showHelp precedes the allocation/use.
limitations: The -o/-a output-path choice is the local user's own CLI input (same privilege); no path-traversal privilege boundary exists in this code, so no CWE-22 finding was raised.

`fread(header, 1, 8, hMP4File)` return value is unchecked; if fewer than 8 bytes are read, `header[4..7]` comparisons consume uninitialized stack bytes (CWE-908) and the eight consecutive `ungetc` calls push more characters than the one C guarantees without intervening reads. These cause at most a wrong branch (raw vs mp4 decode) or UB in the same-privilege process, with no demonstrated corruption or disclosure, so they were not promoted to primary.
Repeated `-o`/`-a` options leak the earlier allocation; a leak only, no security impact.

Impact is limited to contexts where argv strings are attacker-influenced (e.g., wrapper scripts or file managers passing crafted arguments); for a purely interactive CLI the same user already controls their own process.

verdict.summary: png_zalloc divides by the unchecked callback parameter `size` (line 14) before any zero check; a zalloc request with size==0 (any representable uInt value per the callback's full declared domain, reachable from attacker-controlled decompression parameters) causes an integer division by zero and aborts the process parsing attacker-supplied PNG data (denial of service). The adjacent multiplication overflow check itself is otherwise correct.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the divisor `size` is an attacker-data parameter (uInt, full domain including 0) consumed with no zero/emptiness check anywhere in the function; the mention sweep (lines 14, 19) found no guard. Instantiated trigger: caller of the zalloc callback supplies items=1, size=0; evaluation of PNG_UINT_32_MAX/0 raises a divide exception (SIGFPE), crashing the process that parses attacker-controlled PNG/zlib data — a denial of service.

assumptions: uInt is a 32-bit unsigned type, so 0 is representable in size's declared domain; png_zalloc is a memory-allocation callback registered with zlib, making its parameters attacker-data per the width-domain model.
limitations: Impact is a crash/DoS only (no memory corruption, disclosure, or bypass); if a reviewer treats the caller (zlib) as contractually forbidden from passing size==0, that contract is not quoted in this code and per the rules cannot dismiss the candidate.

The png_malloc NULL return is tested at line 26 only under the PNG_1_0_X build; in other builds NULL is returned to the caller rather than dereferenced here, so no local defect was recorded for that path.

verdict.summary: pktRemoveEvidence validates the attacker-controlled evidence index with `idx <= area->evidence().size()` instead of `idx < size()`, allowing a one-past-the-end index (and index 0 on an empty list) to be passed to area->deleteEvidence(idx), which performs an out-of-bounds container element removal/destruction reachable from a network client.

All attacker-data sinks in ProcXResQueryResourceBytes are guarded: the numSpecs product is overflow-checked with the correct operator and unit ('stuff->numSpecs > UINT32_MAX / sizeof(ctx.specs[0])' admits at most numSpecs=0x1FFFFFFF, product 0xFFFFFFF8, no wrap, and rejects 0x20000000), REQUEST_FIXED_SIZE binds numSpecs to bytes physically present in the request, the ctx setup carries an allocation-failure arm (return BadAlloc) before any use, and callee output is gated by 'if (rc == Success)'. No unguarded sink reachable with an in-domain attacker value was found.

assumptions: The syntactically corrupted fragment '... (void*) ((char*) stuff + sz_xXResQueryResourceBytesReq))) { return BadAlloc; }' is interpreted as the remnant of a checked initialization call of the form 'if (!SetupCtx(&ctx, stuff->numSpecs, (void*)((char*)stuff + sz_xXResQueryResourceBytesReq))) { return BadAlloc; }', i.e. ctx (including ctx.specs/nspecs and ctx.response) is initialized before ConstructResourceBytes is invoked.

Callees not shown (ConstructResourceBytes, WriteFragmentsToClient, DestroyConstructResourceBytesCtx) are assumed to be the standard X server implementations; the raw XID stuff->client is validated inside ConstructResourceBytes and its failure is locally consumed via the checked 'rc == Success' gate.
Swapped requests are byte-swapped by the SProc dispatcher before reaching this Proc handler, as is standard in the X server dispatch design.
limitations: The ctx-initialization fragment is syntactically invalid as printed; if it in fact fails to initialize ctx.specs/nspecs/response, an uninitialized-stack-struct defect (CWE-457) would exist, but that cannot be instantiated from the given text since the BadAlloc error arm and its argument list imply a checked setup call.

A 32-bit build (size_t == 32 bits) could wrap 'sizeof(req) + numSpecs*8' inside REQUEST_FIXED_SIZE for numSpecs near 0x1FFFFFFF, but triggering requires a ~4GB request that the request-length and buffer domains of such builds bound below; speculative.

rep.length = bytes_to_int32(ctx.resultBytes) could truncate if resultBytes exceeded ~16GB, but resultBytes is accumulated from server-side resource sizes, not from an attacker-scalable value in this code; speculative.

Validation of the target client XID (stuff->client) against the clients[] table occurs inside the not-shown callee ConstructResourceBytes; this code does check the returned status before using any callee output.

verdict.summary: The attacker-controlled 'logout' request parameter (url) is validated by the quoted error-arm guard 'oidc_validate_post_logout_url(...) == FALSE -> HTTP_BAD_REQUEST' in execution order before every downstream use (post_logout_redirect_uri construction and final oidc_handle_logout_request); the NULL/empty arm substitutes the admin-configured default_slo_url, and end_session construction applies oidc_util_escape_string plus '?'/&' detection. No trigger with attacker-data reaches a sink without the quoted guard.

assumptions: oidc_validate_post_logout_url is assumed to enforce the post-logout URL policy (scheme/hostname check introduced by the CVE-2021-37589 fix); its internals are not shown, but its invocation with the error arm returning HTTP_BAD_REQUEST is quoted and correctly positioned before both sinks.

oidc_is_front_channel_logout / oidc_is_back_channel_logout are assumed to restrict the front/back-channel branches to the module's own configured logout URIs (unshown callees); these branches do not pass the raw url onward to a redirect in the back-channel case.
limitations: Front-channel branch passes the raw, unvalidated url to oidc_handle_logout_request; an open redirect there would require the unshown helpers to both accept an out-of-pattern URL and redirect to it — two unverifiable steps, so this stays speculative.
oidc_debug(r, "enter (url=%s)", url) logs raw attacker data; newline injection (log forging, CWE-117) is possible only if the unshown oidc_debug/ap_log_rerror path does not sanitize.
url may be NULL when passed to oidc_is_front_channel_logout/oidc_is_back_channel_logout before the NULL check; a NULL-unsafe callee would yield at most a same-privilege crash (robustness).
error_str/error_description are consumed in the error arm on the FALSE path; if the unshown validator returned FALSE without filling them, the impact is limited to a degraded error page.

verdict.summary: In nfs3svc_decode_writeargs, the sole data-sufficiency check `if (dlen < XDR_QUADLEN(len)*4)` is defeated by 32-bit unsigned wrap: XDR_QUADLEN(len)=((len+3)>>2) evaluates to 0 for len in {0xFFFFFFFD,0xFFFFFFFE,0xFFFFFFFF}, so a WRITE request with count=len=0xFFFFFFFD and no payload passes. The subsequent clamp silently re-labels len to max_blocksize instead of rejecting, and the kvec loop maps rq_pages[] entries never backed by received data; the write path then consumes up to max_blocksize bytes of NULL/stale pages, causing a remote kernel crash or disclosure of kernel memory into an attacker-readable file.

evidence.reason: Root cause: this is the only statement verifying that the received message actually carried `len` bytes, but XDR_QUADLEN(len)*4 wraps to 0 for len >= 0xFFFFFFFD ((len+3) overflows 32-bit unsigned), making `dlen < 0` always false. Trigger: NFSv3 WRITE with count=len=0xFFFFFFFD and zero payload passes this check, is clamped to max_blocksize at line 44, and the loop at lines 49-54 builds rq_vec over pages that hold no received data.

Taint origin: `len` is an attacker-supplied u32 from the network WRITE request; any representable value including 0xFFFFFFFD is instantiable, and no statement between this line and the line-39 check bounds it.

assumptions: svc_max_payload(rqstp) returns a value within the capacity of rq_vec/rq_pages arrays, so the clamp at lines 42-45 keeps the loop index v in-bounds of the arrays.

nfsd3_proc_write consumes rqstp->rq_vec[0..args->vlen-1] and args->count as the write payload without re-verifying against received length; this is the documented contract of the rq_vec/vlen/count outputs this decoder builds.
XDR_QUADLEN is the standard macro ((l)+3)>>2 evaluated in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic.
limitations: The concrete downstream consequence (kernel NULL deref/DoS vs. stale-page information disclosure) depends on the state of rq_pages[] entries beyond the received message, which the RPC receive layer (not shown) controls; either outcome is a direct security impact from the same defect.

decode_fh and xdr_decode_hyper read from p before the line-17 head-bounds check; if a truncated message lets these reads pass head->iov_len, they remain within the page-backed head buffer and the function returns 0 at line 17 — robustness, not a security impact.
args->stable is not range-checked here; downstream treatment of out-of-range stable values was not shown and appears functional, not security-relevant.

verdict.summary: Both branches of fp48_write_bin are guarded by exact-equality length checks — `if (len != 32 * RLC_FP_BYTES)` (packed) and `if (len != 48 * RLC_FP_BYTES)` (unpacked) — that throw before any write and admit only the exact byte count each branch writes (4x8*RLC_FP_BYTES = 32*RLC_FP_BYTES packed; 2x24*RLC_FP_BYTES = 48*RLC_FP_BYTES unpacked), so no out-of-bounds write is reachable with any value of len. All reads of `a` use in-bounds indices of the declared fp48_t type. The only anomaly — the packed branch serializing components of `a` rather than the fp48_pck output `t` — is at most a serialization correctness defect whose security impact requires an unshown consumer and is recorded in notes.limitations.

evidence.reason: Decisive guard: exact-equality check on len, executed before all four packed writes; admits only len == 32*RLC_FP_BYTES, exactly the 4 x 8*RLC_FP_BYTES bytes written at lines 14-17, so no len value in the size_t domain can make any fp8_write_bin write out of bounds (the analogous 48*RLC_FP_BYTES guard at lines 19-21 covers the unpacked branch).

assumptions: fp8_write_bin and fp24_write_bin serialize exactly 8*RLC_FP_BYTES and 24*RLC_FP_BYTES bytes respectively (fixed-width tower types fp8 = 8 and fp24 = 24 base-field elements), matching the len arguments passed at every call site.
RLC_THROW(ERR_NO_BUFFER) performs a non-local exit out of RLC_TRY, so the writes are skipped whenever a length check fails.
fp48_new/RLC_ALLOC reports allocation failure per RELIC convention; even if it returned NULL, the result is only a same-privilege crash in fp48_pck.
limitations: The packed branch writes a[0][1], a[0][2], a[1][0], a[1][2] (lines 14-17) instead of the compressed t produced by fp48_pck(t, a) (line 13). If fp48_pck transforms the value (rather than validate-and-copy), the serialized 'packed' bytes contain unpacked components and fp48_read_bin(pack=1) would reconstruct a wrong element. Memory-safe here (fixed sizes, in-bounds reads); the security impact depends on an unshown downstream consumer, so per STEP 4 it is not promoted.

The snippet ends mid-RLC_TRY with no RLC_CATCH/RLC_FINALLY/fp48_free(t); if fp48_free is genuinely absent in the full function, t leaks per call (CWE-401), but this appears to be a truncation artifact and the per-call leak size is fixed with call frequency not controlled in this code.
The missing sentinel test on fp48_new(t) is at worst a NULL-dereference crash of the same-privileged process; no corruption, disclosure, or bypass is shown.

verdict.summary: rv10_decode_packet validates the attacker-controlled slice position and macroblock count with correctly oriented, execution-ordered guards (POS check on s->mb_x/s->mb_y upper bounds and the mb_count>left COUNT check), so the macroblock decode loop provably stays inside the frame. Remaining candidates (buf_size*8 wrap, 8*buf_size2 gb expansion, mb_x-1 underflow at ff_er_add_slice, negative mb coordinates) all require unshown caller/callee behavior to produce harm and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: s->mb_width, s->mb_height, s->mb_stride, s->b8_stride are positive values fixed at decoder init before this function runs; all frame-position arithmetic (mb_pos, left) stays within int range for any codec-legal dimensions.
ff_h263_decode_mb, MPV_decode_mb, ff_er_frame_end/start, MPV_frame_start, ff_set_qscale, ff_er_add_slice are FFmpeg-internal callees whose per-calls invariants are not shown in this snippet.
limitations: init_get_bits(&s->gb, buf, buf_size*8) ignores the return and buf_size*8 can wrap to INT_MIN for a >=256MB packet (buf_size=268435456); however the checked bitstream reader then stalls and the error path returns -1, so no memory-safety impact is instantiated inside this code.

s->gb.size_in_bits is expanded to 8*buf_size2, letting bit reads continue past the initially declared buf_size*8; safety relies on the demuxer guaranteeing buf_size2 readable bytes at buf, a contract not quotable here. An upstream caller violating it could cause an out-of-bounds read; not instantiable from this code.

ff_er_add_slice is called with endx = s->mb_x-1, which is -1 when mb_count==0 at mb_x==0 or when the final decoded macroblock completes a row; no local check exists, but the endx<0 consumption occurs entirely inside the not-shown callee (historically guarded by a startx>endx rejection), so no impact link is characterizable here.

The POS check quotes only upper bounds; a negative s->mb_x or s->mb_y set by the not-shown picture-header decoders would pass it and inflate 'left'. Instantiating this requires the header decoder to emit a negative coordinate from a bit reader (producer not shown) and the OOB write inside not-shown decode callees, so it remains speculative.
s->qscale from the not-shown header decoders is passed to ff_set_qscale without a local range check; table-index safety depends on the callee, which is not shown.

verdict.summary: GlyphCache::Loader parses attacker-controlled font tables, but every in-code memory sink is guarded by a quoted, execution-order-verified size check: the 8-byte Gloc header read is covered by 'm_pGloc.size() < 8', the 4-byte Glat version read by 'm_pGlat.size() < 4', the second 4-byte Glat read by '(version >= 0x00030000 && m_pGlat.size() < 8)', and the attacker-influenced size arithmetic in tmpnumgattrs (which can wrap when flags&0x2 with a large _num_attrs and small Gloc) provably converts to a negative int that the 'tmpnumgattrs < 0' reject arm catches before any use. The remaining candidate, _num_glyphs_graphics-1 underflowing to size_t(-1) when GlyphCount returns 0, passes an out-of-range index into the not-shown TtfUtil::LocaLookup, but this code tests the failure sentinel '== size_t(-2)' before any use of the return and the only harmful use would occur inside the unshown callee, so the impact is not instantiated here.

assumptions: size_t-to-int conversion of out-of-range values uses the low 32 bits (mainstream gcc/clang/MSVC ABI); under this the wrapped tmpnumgattrs is always negative, which the 'tmpnumgattrs < 0' check rejects. The wrap cannot yield a small positive value because sizeof(uint16)*_num_attrs <= 131070 < 2^31.
Face::Table::size() and operator bool behave as read-only size/validity accessors with no side effects affecting the guards.
TtfUtil::GlyphCount returns a value in the uint16 domain, matching the ~unsigned-short member _num_glyphs_graphics.
limitations: numGlyphs == 0 (in-domain value from attacker-controlled maxp) makes '_num_glyphs_graphics-1' evaluate to size_t(-1), which is passed to the not-shown TtfUtil::LocaLookup (line 21). This code checks the returned sentinel '== size_t(-2)' before any use, and the comment 'This will fail if the number of glyphs is wildly out of range' documents the callee's range-check contract (with _loca.size() passed as an explicit bound), but the callee body is not shown; if LocaLookup mishandles size_t(-1), the out-of-bounds read would occur there, not in this code.
TtfUtil::GlyphCount(maxp) may read beyond a truncated maxp table; the read occurs inside the not-shown callee, so no impact is instantiated here.

When the glyf table is absent, the 'if (_glyf && ...)' short-circuit skips the LocaLookup validation and _num_glyphs_graphics (0-65535, attacker-controlled) remains otherwise unvalidated in this constructor; downstream consumers of that field are not shown.
When dumb_font is true, the entire Glat/Gloc validation block is skipped by design; no use of the unvalidated values occurs within this snippet.
'_has_boxes = true;' (compiler workaround) forces the boxes format regardless of glatflags; any downstream misinterpretation of the Glat table would occur in code not shown here.

verdict.summary: png_zalloc divides by the callback parameter `size` in the overflow check `items > PNG_UINT_32_MAX/size` without any zero-check; size is a data-carrying parameter of a zlib allocation callback whose full unsigned-int domain includes 0, and no statement in the code validates it before the division, so size=0 causes a division-by-zero fault (denial of service in the process consuming the compressed stream).

evidence.reason: Division by attacker-domain callback parameter `size` with no zero-check anywhere in the function; trigger size=0 (representable uInt) reaches this line unguarded and faults. Root cause: missing `size == 0` guard before the division.

evidence.snippet: png_zalloc(voidpf png_ptr, uInt items, uInt size)
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: `size` is a data-carrying parameter of this exported zlib zalloc callback; its full declared domain (unsigned int, including 0) is the attack surface, and no local validation narrows it before the division at line 11.

assumptions: png_zalloc is invoked as a zlib zalloc callback, so its parameters are judged at full declared width per the callback attacker-data rule; `size` is not produced or constrained by any statement in this code.
PNG_UINT_32_MAX is the 32-bit unsigned maximum, so the overflow guard itself is otherwise arithmetically correct (verified at both bounds).
limitations: Misordered NULL check: `png_uint_32 save_flags=p->flags;` (line 5) dereferences png_ptr before `if (png_ptr == NULL) return (NULL);` (lines 9-10); a NULL png_ptr crashes at line 5 before the guard runs. Classified as robustness (same-privilege crash, no corruption/bypass) per the NULL-dereference impact rule, not the verdict; the producer of png_ptr is the library's own registration pointer, not attacker data.
Real-world reachability of size=0 depends on zlib's internal zalloc call sites, which are not shown; the trigger is instantiated from the callback parameter domain, not from a quoted caller path.

The memset block (lines 23-31) is compiled only under PNG_1_0_X && !PNG_NO_ZALLOC_ZERO; when compiled out, a NULL png_malloc return is passed to zlib unchecked here, which is zlib's documented contract to test.
